sections.label: Investing in youth, culture, sports
sections.summary: It is time to invest more in youth, culture and sports to nurture national identity, forge an unconquerable soul and give hope and unity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: But that would clearly be wrong, it would be a mistake.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: It is time now to invest more, even double down, and harness the good and positive energy that our youth, as well as our cultural and sporting activities can provide – to help us nurture a stronger national identity, forge an unconquerable soul and be a source of hope and unity for Singaporeans even as our nation charts a new course in a COVID-stricken world and prepares itself for a post-COVID-19 one.

sections.label: Income inequality and poverty
sections.summary: National income distribution remains embarrassing versus high-income peers, and the poor are estimated at up to a quarter of the population.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While we have slowly chipped away at extreme inequality that characterise earnings just prior to the global crisis of 2007, the distribution of our national income, even after accounting for taxes and transfers, remains embarrassing when compared to our high-income peers.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The number of poor in our midst informally defined because we have steadfastly refused to define an official poverty line.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is flattered by our very conservative definition of basic needs, and even so it is estimated at as much as as a quarter of the population.

sections.label: Minimum Wage and Workfare
sections.summary: The passage argues policy balance is skewed, and proposes universal Minimum Wage and negative income tax via Workfare.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Remarkably, our policy balance has now become so skewed that we could potentially garner significant gains in terms of improving equity and by extension national welfare, with minimal losses in terms of foregone efficiency.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: All we need is the courage of our convictions.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We have a form of Minimum Wage policy via the Progressive Wage Model.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet until, recently, we had deemed it unwise to make it universal and still dress the policy with so many additional conditions that the incentives for upskilling turn into loopholes the employers use to retain workers on the lowest rung of wages.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We warn against unaffordable costs and lost jobs despite evidence that the majority of Singaporeans would be willing to pay more for essential services and that the employment impact of a Minimum Wage is likely to be very limited.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We propose a form of negative income tax via Workfare, but the nature of Earned Income Tax Credit programmes such as this, is that it compels work.

sections.label: ComCare and Kindergarten Fee Assistance
sections.summary: The passage states more policies like ComCare and the Kindergarten Fee Assistance Scheme are needed.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: What we need are more policies like ComCare and the Kindergarten Fee Assistance Scheme, both of which have made substantive steps towards bolstering our sense of opportunity and care for others in our society.

sections.label: Commit to Compassionate Policy-Making
sections.summary: The passage calls for committing to compassionate policy-making principles and setting out plans now.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Let us commit to the principles of compassionate policy-making now and set out plans in the moment.

sections.label: Compassionate Policy-Making for Singaporeans
sections.summary: The passage states Singaporeans face the crisis without tried and tested social safety nets, so focus should protect workers, opportunities and ideas.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Singaporeans are faced not only with the need to tighten their belts to weather the storm, they are also confronted with the uncomfortable conundrum of facing this unprecedented event without the reassurance of tried and tested social safety nets that are rather commonplace in other advanced economies.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is imperative, therefore, the our focus is on protecting workers though not necessarily jobs; opportunities and not only businesses; ideas and not ideologies.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Compassionate policy-making then requires a keen understanding of the plight of others and a recognition that our policies have deep implications for the lived reality of ordinary Singaporeans.

sections.label: Temper Majority Interest with Minority
sections.summary: The passage states majority interest should be tempered with concern for the minority.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Ultimately, we should temper majority interest with a concern for the minority as well.

sections.label: Poverty Line, Minimum Wage, CPF
sections.summary: The passage says low-wage foreign worker reliance needs scrutiny, and proposes an official poverty line, Minimum Wage and CPF flexibility.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But it is also recognising that the conditions in which they have been enduring are inappropriate for a First World country such as ours.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is about acknowledging that our economic model, which continues to rely on low-wage foreign workers such as these, is a clear blind spot that can stand for more scrutiny.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We can introduce an official poverty line closely linked to ComCare.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We can implement a simple across-the-board Minimum Wage, and we can introduce more flexibility to our access to our CPF monies.

sections.label: Minimum Wage job loss risk
sections.summary: A universal Minimum Wage in a recession risks many lower wage workers losing their jobs, going from low-wage to no-wage.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
sentences.text: In current times, where businesses are being challenged and we are in a period of recession, there is a very real risk that if we were to introduce a universal Minimum Wage across all sectors, I think many of our lower wage workers may lose their jobs, and from low-wage they become no-wage.

sections.label: Agreeing Minimum Wage principle in crisis
sections.summary: The speaker argues a Minimum Wage can be agreed in principle during the crisis and rolled out after the storm passes.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: The truth is, I would argue that we should be able to think about implementing policies like a Minimum Wage in a time of crisis because this concentrates the mind.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: If we agree in principle, as I said in my speech, with the idea of a Minimum Wage, which is one step to the left, a half-step perhaps of the Progressive Wage Model; in fact, that Minimum Wage policy, once we agree on that, can be easily rolled out after the storm has passed.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: So, there is no doubt that at this very moment, such a policy may not be ideal, but let us come together and agree that this is a principle that we want to roll out.

sections.label: Low-wage workers' real wage rise
sections.summary: Over the last five years, low-wage workers' wages rose by 30% in real terms.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
sentences.text: In the last five years, our low-wage workers have seen wages rise by 30% in real terms.

sections.label: Expanding Progressive Wage Model announced
sections.summary: In March this year, as part of the Budget, the speaker announced looking at expanding PWM.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
sentences.text: In this House, in March this year, as part of the Budget, and I too announced that we are looking at expanding PWM.

sections.label: Four Budgets in three months
sections.summary: The Government put up four Budgets in the space of three months.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
sentences.text: If you talk about compassion, we have just put up four Budgets in the space of three months.

sections.label: Workfare transfers to low-wage workers
sections.summary: Workfare involves the Government putting in revenues to transfer back to low-wage workers.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
sentences.text: As to the part about not recognising what the Government has done, if you are to look at the low-wage workers of today, beyond just wages, how we have helped both the industries as well as the consumers – the people out there – if you discount the fact that the Workfare comes to play where the Government puts in revenues to transfer back to workers of low wages.

sections.label: Low-wage workers home ownership
sections.summary: About 70% of the bottom 20% of workers own their own homes today.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
sentences.text: Among our low-wage workers, the bottom 20% of all our workers, about 70% of them own their own homes today.

sections.label: Median wages, national income, NUS study
sections.summary: Median wages have risen but national income rose faster, and the low-wage study came from NUS.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: With regard to real wages, it is true that median wages have risen in this country and that is in fact a good thing.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: But unfortunately, national income has risen much faster, and as a result, in spite of this progress — Think of it this way, imagine that there is a pie.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: The Member also asked me about where the low-wage study came from.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: But basically, it is a study from the National University of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: I was heartened to see, in fact, that the Times Higher Education Supplement recently ranked NUS as among the top 25 universities globally.

sections.label: Appropriate Minimum Wage level
sections.summary: It asks what level of Minimum Wage the Member proposes is appropriate for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: First, what is the level of Minimum Wage that the Member proposes is appropriate for Singapore?

sections.label: Appropriate Minimum Wage level
sections.summary: It states the first question is what the appropriate level of the Minimum Wage is.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: The first is what is the appropriate level of the Minimum Wage.

sections.label: Panel to evaluate Minimum Wage
sections.summary: The panel should continue yearly after the Minimum Wage policy is rolled out to evaluate whether the level is appropriate.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: In fact, that panel should continue to exist year after year after that Minimum Wage policy is rolled out because that would allow us to continually evaluate whether the level of the Minimum Wage is appropriate.

sections.label: Minimum Wage and unemployment studies
sections.summary: Raw unemployment rates should not be compared across countries, and studies show Minimum Wage has minimal or statistically insignificant unemployment impact.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: As for countries with different levels of unemployment, I think it is imperative for me to clarify that we do not want to be comparing raw unemployment rates across countries willy-nilly.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: But what I will say is this – the basis for me to argue that Minimum Wage has a very limited impact on unemployment is premised on reams and reams of studies.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: Studies within the economics profession have repeatedly shown that in almost every instance, the unemployment impact is either very minimal or statistically insignificant such that it cannot be detected in a regular statistical test.

sections.label: Town Council minimum wage
sections.summary: The Town Council is being taken over, so no decisions have been made on its minimum wage.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: In terms of the Town Council, well, as you know, we are in the process of taking over the Town Council so we have not made decisions on the minimum wage for the Town Council.

sections.label: Singapore not borrowing in pandemic
sections.summary: Singapore is said to be among the very few countries, maybe the only one, that has not borrowed in pandemic times.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: I hope you are not teaching that in your classes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: But to my knowledge, Singapore is one of the very few countries in the world, maybe the only one that has not got to borrow in such pandemic times.

sections.label: Average household basic needs expenditure
sections.summary: A 2019 Government answer put average household expenditure on basic needs at $1,300 per month, versus $1,250 in an earlier reply.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In response to a separate Parliamentary Question that we asked – what is the average household expenditure on basic needs – we asked this of the Government, I believe, in 2019 and the answer came back – $1,300 per month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: When a similar question was asked by my colleague Mr Gerald Giam, the answer was $1,250 per month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If I recall correctly, that was a number of years back.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, $1,300 per month is the average household expenditure on basic needs.

sections.label: Workers below basic needs expenditure
sections.summary: The question asks what to say to individuals earning under $1,300 monthly while supporting a household below average basic needs expenditure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Minister of State and others have said that the Progressive Wage Models can be rolled out to more sectors but my question to Minister of State Zaqy would really be – what would you say to individuals earning less than $1,300 per month who are supporting a household which is below the average household expenditure on basic needs that the Government itself has specified.

sections.label: Raising lowest paid workers' wages
sections.summary: The Government believes raising lowest paid workers' wages matters, cites progress, and describes the PWM as Minimum Wage-plus and sectoral.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
sentences.text: First, I would like to say, on behalf of the Government, that we do believe that it is important to raise the wages of our lowest paid workers.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
sentences.text: We have achieved significant progress in the last 10 years and in the last five years.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
sentences.text: The PWM is a Minimum Wage-plus and it is a sectoral approach.

sections.label: Progressive Wage Model and subsidies
sections.summary: Wage earners' pride in a job and wage is preserved through the Progressive Wage Model, which must be expanded, and other subsidies.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
sentences.text: How do we do it without losing that wage earners' ability to have the pride of having a job and earning a wage?

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
sentences.text: We do it through the Progressive Wage Model, which has to be expanded.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
sentences.text: We do it through a range of other subsidies – whether it is KiFAS, the housing subsidies and many other ways.

sections.label: Woman scammed of life savings
sections.summary: She was scammed of more than $10,000, a substantial part of her life savings.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Just like that, she was scammed of more than $10,000, a substantial part of her life savings.

sections.label: Online bullying, risks and scams
sections.summary: Surveys and studies show online bullying, online risks among youths, and scams doubling in the first half of 2020 with almost 8,000 scams and $103 million cheated.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: A 2018 survey commissioned by Mediacorp’s Talking Point showed that three out of four youths between the ages of 13 and 19 have been bullied online.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Based on a study by Microsoft in 2019, two in three Singapore youths between the ages of 13 and 17 have encountered at least one form of online risk, including exposure to unwanted sexual content.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Online scams doubled in the first half of 2020, compared to the same period last year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: There were almost 8,000 scams, with a staggering $103 million cheated.

sections.label: No single agency on online harm
sections.summary: No single agency is responsible for preventing online harm, different agencies handle different aspects, and a coordinating agency is needed.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Today, no single agency bears the responsibility of preventing and mitigating online harm.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Correspondingly, different Government agencies grasp different aspects of the issue: MOE for cyberwellness education in schools; MCI for digital literacy for seniors and media literacy for young adults; MSF for counselling and support for victims through voluntary welfare organisations; and MCCY for youth mental well-being.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: This approach must change, so that we can adapt to the growing complexity of the problem.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: We need a Government agency to step forward, take charge and develop a citizen-centric perspective on this issue.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Like its overseas counterparts, this agency should champion and coordinate the Government’s effort in this area and take the lead in assembling a multi-stakeholder response.

sections.label: Safety by Design for digital services
sections.summary: Companies delivering digital services should adopt Safety by Design and embed safety features from the outset.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: First, companies that deliver digital services should be more thoughtful in the design of their products.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: They should adopt the concept of “Safety by Design” and embed safety features from the outset as part of the design process.

sections.label: National movement for online space
sections.summary: A new national movement under SG Together for the online space is proposed, citing the NTU student initiative Flag, You're It!.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: Perhaps, it is timely for us to have a new national movement under SG Together for the online space.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: A good example is “Flag, You’re It!”, an initiative by a group of NTU students to campaign against cyber grooming.

sections.label: Government support for national movement
sections.summary: The Government can convene platforms and amplify ground-up efforts through funding and mentoring support.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: The Government can support this national movement by convening platforms to bring together such like-minded parties and amplify these ground-up efforts through funding and mentoring support.

sections.label: Agency to coordinate government policies
sections.summary: A government agency should coordinate policies and appoint a panel of professionals to study the issue and recommend to the government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: First, we need a government agency to coordinate and bring together the various government policies and efforts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
sentences.text: The agency can appoint a panel that comprises professionals and for the panel to study the issue in a holistic manner and make relevant recommendations to the government.

sections.label: Worst recession since Independence
sections.summary: Singapore faces its worst recession since Independence, with GDP shrinking 13.2% year on year and employment falling 131,500 workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As pointed out by Mdm President, we are facing our worst recession since Independence and we have already seen Singapore's GDP shrink by 13.2% year on year in the second quarter, with total employment seeing the largest quarterly decline on record at 131,500 workers.

sections.label: Rethink societal values and progress
sections.summary: The Government is called to measure national progress holistically and base policy on overall well-being, especially of the most vulnerable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is perhaps time for us to have a rethink of what we value as a society and who have we left behind in our pursuit of headline economic growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I call on the Government to evaluate its success not just based on a set of economic terms, but to take a more holistic, multi-dimensional approach in measuring the progress of our nation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We should base our policy decision-making on not just maximising financial value, but on maximising the overall well-being of all Singaporeans, particularly the most vulnerable amongst us.

sections.label: Job vacancies to unemployed ratio
sections.summary: The ratio of job vacancies to unemployed persons hit a historical low of .71 as at March 2020, with demand outlook poor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The ratio of job vacancies to unemployed persons reached a historical low of .71 as at March 2020 and with the demand outlook remaining poor and arguably the worst of retrenchments and unemployment perhaps still ahead of us.

sections.label: Housing needs and flat value
sections.summary: The Minister for National Development wrote about housing needs, but HDB resale market is affected by lease decay concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In its Addendum to the President's Address, the Minister for National Development wrote about taking care of Singaporeans' housing needs, such as ensuring that public housing remains affordable, especially for young families, while enhancing schemes to help our seniors tap on their flats' value to supplement their retirement adequacy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, it is precisely our flats' value that is in question where the HDB resale market has been affected by concerns over lease decay in the past few years.

sections.label: Singaporeans in HDB flats
sections.summary: More than 80% of Singaporeans live in HDB flats, with most relying on CPF Ordinary Account balances to finance their flats.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Ultimately, more than 80% of Singaporeans live in HDB flats, with the overwhelming majority relying on their CPF Ordinary Account balances to finance their flats.

sections.label: Record low fertility rate
sections.summary: Singapore's Total Fertility Rate is at a record low of 1.14 in 2019, and couples may delay marriage and parenthood amid economic uncertainties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Singapore's Total Fertility Rate stands at a record low of 1.14 in 2019 and many couples could potentially be further delaying their marriage and parenthood plans amidst the economic uncertainties today.

sections.label: Legislative right to flexible work
sections.summary: The passage states more can be done and that employees need a legislative right to flexible work arrangements rather than non-legally binding advisories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet, there is so much more that we can do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We need to give employees the legislative right to flexible work arrangements rather than non-legally binding advisories.

sections.label: Land sales and investment returns
sections.summary: The passage states a revenue shortfall could be met by tapping no more than a fifth of about $15 billion yearly land sales or raising Net Investment Returns Contribution by up to 10%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As such, one of the ways that the revenue shortfall could potentially be met is by tapping no more than a fifth of the approximately $15 billion per year in land sales that the Government typically collects.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The other area that could potentially be looked at as an alternative source of revenue is to increase the Net Investment Returns Contribution by up to 10%.

sections.label: Strengthening employment laws for workers
sections.summary: The passage states it is time to strengthen employment laws to protect workers' interests and carry out sustained structural reforms for better financial security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Singapore Government has always been proud of the pro-business environment created through economic and manpower policies, but I feel that it is time for us to strengthen our employment laws to better protect workers' interests and take this opportunity to carry out sustained and structural reforms to ensure that our workers enjoy better financial security.

sections.label: Expiring HDB leases and resale prices
sections.summary: The passage states expiring leases have affected HDB resale prices, and declining prices as leases end cause mental stress and loss of security for Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Leases that are about to expire has affected the resale price of HDB flats in recent years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For many Singaporeans, their main asset is their HDB flat, and they have spent most of their life savings on it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, if Singaporeans, upon entering their golden years, see resale prices declining gradually as the lease of their flat coming to an end, they would feel mentally stressed and lose the sense of security, because the HDB flat can no longer ensure that they have sufficient retirement funds.

sections.label: Land sales revenue and reserves growth
sections.summary: The passage states land sales average $15 billion yearly but are excluded from the budget, and the Workers' Party proposes slowing reserves' growth rate, not raiding reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For example, every year, we make an average of $15 billion from land sales, but these revenues are not included in the Government's budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I must stress that what the Workers' Party is proposing is not raiding our reserves, but to slow the reserves' growth rate.

sections.label: Echo chambers and understanding
sections.summary: The passage says echo chambers entrench views and that society must shift from tolerance to active understanding of different views.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Echo chambers where entrenched views take root and we end up in shouting matches on opposite ends of divisive issues.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: We got here by emphasising tolerance and mutual respect, and while mutual respect will always be relevant, we must navigate the uncomfortable but necessary shift from mere tolerance, past acceptance, to active understanding of different views.

sections.label: Singapore women's progress
sections.summary: Within a few decades Singapore became a place where girls attend university, join the workforce and run for political candidacy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Only a few decades have passed and now Singapore is a place where girls go to university, participate in the workforce and run for political candidacy.

sections.label: Old versus young framing
sections.summary: Pitting old against young obfuscates common ground and can cause workplace tensions with three to four generations under one roof.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: They obfuscate the path to finding common ground by pitting old versus young.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: This can cause tensions in the workplace as the average office environment now houses three to four generations under one roof.

sections.label: Singapore's post-war transformation
sections.summary: Singapore became a bustling metropolis instead of an abandoned port city, fulfilling citizens' stake through education, home equity and wage growth.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The unlikely reality of Singapore building a bustling metropolis in place of what could have been an abandoned port city post war rife with ideological, economic and social strife came to past, and with that, came the promise of a stake in a young nation's progress fulfilled with citizens through education, home equity and wage growth.

sections.label: Generation's mobility worries
sections.summary: The speaker's generation worries about rising home prices, stagnating wages and a competitive job market possibly reducing upward mobility.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Across the world, my generation worries about rising home prices, stagnating wages and an increasingly competitive job market that could mean that we will not see the same rate of upward mobility as that of generations before.

sections.label: SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways programme
sections.summary: The Government introduced the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways programme offering 14,500 opportunities, with full-time trainees receiving a monthly allowance.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The Government recently introduced the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways programme.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The programme aims to provide 14,500 opportunities for mid-career jobseekers to gain meaningful industry-relevant experience.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Those part of the full-time training programme will receive a monthly allowance.

sections.label: Rental flat fee increase
sections.summary: Rental flat fees could rise up to eight times with household income, and a fixed fee for longer is suggested.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The rental flat fees could increase by up to eight times, depending on the increase in household income.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Could we consider a fixed rental fee for a longer period of time to allow such households to build up their savings for rainier days and future dreams?

sections.label: MSF social assistance addendum
sections.summary: Minister Masagos Zulkifli outlined the government's focus on improving social assistance for families needing more comprehensive, coordinated services.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In the Ministry of Social and Family Development’s addendum, Minister Masagos Zulkifli outlined the government’s focus on improving social assistance so that families who need it can receive services that are more comprehensive and coordinated.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I welcome this effort as it enhances the government’s reach to connect residents to the last-mile service delivery.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I acknowledge that assistance given in a timely manner can change one’s life.

sections.label: Global carbon emissions drop
sections.summary: At the peak of worldwide lockdowns in early April, global daily carbon emissions fell 17% to 2006 levels.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: At the peak of the lockdowns around the world in early April, global daily carbon emissions were slashed by 17%, dropping to levels last observed in 2006.

sections.label: Punggol family job loss
sections.summary: A Punggol family where both parents lost jobs, partly due to past offences, got by with ComCare and COVID Support grants.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We have a family in Punggol in which both parents lost their jobs and finding new ones was not easy partly because they were past offenders.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: They got by with ComCare and COVID Support grants.

sections.label: Edusave Bursary Award recipients
sections.summary: Two of them even received the Edusave Bursary Award recently.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Two of them even received the Edusave Bursary Award recently.

sections.label: Climate change existential threat
sections.summary: Climate change will remain an existential threat for generations, so sustainability must be a key consideration in all decisions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Climate change will remain an existential threat for many, many generations to come and we must never stop pushing for sustainability as a key consideration in all our decisions.

sections.label: Singapore vulnerability to sea-level rise
sections.summary: Singapore, a low-lying island with limited resources, is vulnerable to rising sea-levels and supply chain disruptions in food and water.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: As a low-lying island with limited natural resources, Singapore is especially vulnerable to rising sea-levels and disruptions in global supply chains of critical resources like food and water.

sections.label: MSE green recovery plans
sections.summary: MSE committed to green recovery plans supporting a low-carbon, climate-resilient future, and will galvanise sustainability efforts, green growth, resource resilience and circular economy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: There is no lack of ideas and energy from all our residents.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We now have a Pasir Ris Sustainability Action Group with over 20 volunteers and growing, from both young and old.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: I am excited now to be in MSE, which has committed to plans for a green recovery from COVID-19, one that supports a transition to a low-carbon and climate-resilient future.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: MSE will galvanise sustainability efforts across the Government, promote green growth, ensure resource resilience and pursue circular economy.

sections.label: Youth-led Somerset Belt Masterplan
sections.summary: The Somerset Belt Masterplan is a youth-led initiative built from ideas of over 40,000 youths, showing what autonomy and trust in youth can produce.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: One initiative that comes to mind is the youth-led Somerset Belt Masterplan, which is a product of the ideas and aspirations of over 40,000 youths on what they wish to see in Somerset and how they can achieve that.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: It is a good example of how innovative concepts and plans can develop when we give autonomy and trust to our youth who can take ownership of the projects they feel strongly for.

sections.label: Listening and engaging youths
sections.summary: The speaker urges listening well and communicating with empathy, citing consulting his two boys on social media to relate to younger generations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Let us learn to listen well to one another, and communicate with more empathy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: Consulting my two boys on the use of social media so that I can relate to the younger generation, I learnt that if I want them to understand me, I need to first connect with them in their channels, sometimes using their language.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: I hope to see better engagement, especially with our youths.

sections.label: Pioneer and Merdeka Generations' achievement
sections.summary: With collaborative efforts from people and Government, the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations made Singapore a prosperous and orderly country.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: With collaborative efforts from the people and the Government, our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations have made Singapore into a prosperous and orderly country.

sections.label: Future Singapore trust or suspicion
sections.summary: The passage asks what kind of Singapore the next generations will build, and whether it will be one of mutual trust or suspicion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: The future will depend on the next generations.” What kind of Singapore are we and our next generations going to build?

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
sentences.text: We must all ask ourselves, do we want a Singapore of mutual trust or suspicion?

sections.label: Economic defence and COVID reserves
sections.summary: MTI ensured food, supplies and resources access, replenished stockpiles, diversified sources and increased local production, while reserves aid the COVID-19 fight.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: In economic defence, the challenges we have met them so far with our various COVID Budgets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Our MTI colleagues have been on the front lines as well, perhaps less unseen than the rest, to ensure that we have sufficient and constant access to food, supplies, resources.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: They have ensured that our stockpiles are replenished, our sources are diversified and local production increased; all this despite global disruptions in supply chains.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Our reserves, which has been spoken so much of during the course of this debate, are also an important weapon and armament in our fight against COVID-19 and its effects.

sections.label: Course and online participation numbers
sections.summary: Over 7,000 people took part in various courses and almost over 20,000 in online interactions during the week.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Over the course of the week, we had over 7,000 people taking part in various courses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: We had almost over 20,000 people taking part in our online interactions as well.

sections.label: Communications, digital inclusion, media literacy
sections.summary: Good communications is key to preventing disease spread, so digital inclusion and media literacy should improve, especially for vulnerable elders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Amidst the crisis that we are experiencing with COVID, it is also a primary concern because good communications is key in preventing the spread of this disease and reducing its impact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: People who decry the use of masks, expounding conspiracy theories figures, fake cures, false advisories, even scams, during this period of time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: It is therefore, no better time than now to improve digital inclusion and media literacy, especially amongst our elders those who are most vulnerable during this period of time.

sections.label: Equal contribution of all Singaporeans
sections.summary: All Singaporeans make an equal contribution to society regardless of how long they have been Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: This idea of you being more Singaporean if you are homegrown or older or spent more years versus those who are newer who have spent less.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: But, all of us make an equal contribution to our society because we are all Singaporeans here, regardless of how long we have been Singaporeans.

sections.label: Crisis as opportunity for Singaporean identity
sections.summary: The crisis is an opportunity to re-emphasise what it means to be Singaporean and why we should be proud of who we are.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: At the same time, there might be others who are very different from us, but in our time of need, can chew us out of that net.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: So for all of us in Singapore, this crisis is an opportunity for us to re-emphasise what it means to be Singaporean, why we should be proud of who we are.

sections.label: Definition of youths in MCCY
sections.summary: MCCY defines youths as those between 15 and 35 years, covering about a quarter of Singapore's population.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In MCCY, we have defined youths as those between 15 and 35 years – sadly excluding myself.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: So, this covers everyone from Secondary school to young adults in their thirties, either just left school or entering the workforce.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This group makes up about a quarter of our population in Singapore.

sections.label: Generational concerns and new Cs
sections.summary: This generation is concerned with climate change, constant competition and caring communities rather than the traditional 5Cs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: While previous generations chased the traditional 5Cs, this generation is concerned with some other Cs – climate change, constant competition and caring communities.

sections.label: COVID-19 care and citizenry
sections.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic animated a spirit of care, cohesion and active citizenry, with ground-up initiatives assisting those in need.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The COVID-19 pandemic has animated a strong spirit of care, cohesion and active citizenry in our society, from ground up, with many organising their own initiatives to assist those in need.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: For example, Project Stable Staples raised $150,000 in funds to give NTUC vouchers to 2,500 individuals they saw and identified as having been affected financially by COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The Youth Corps Singapore volunteers supported food distribution drives and delivered meals to nearly 9,000 beneficiaries.

sections.label: Youth jobs and skills programmes
sections.summary: MCCY, NYC and the National Jobs Council set up schemes for internships, cross-cultural skills, jobs and digital skills for youths.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Together with the National Youth Council or NYC, MCCY has set up a Youth Corps Internship Scheme to allow our students from Institutes of Higher Learning to be placed into on-the-job training to ready themselves for experience for the job eventualy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: NYC has also launched the Asia-Ready Exposure Programe (AEP)	for youths to acquire cross-cultural skills in a global world, that is important, cross-cultural skills to understand the region better, to widen their prospects and with that the range of opportunities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The National Jobs Council is coordinating efforts to provide 100,000 jobs and skills opportunities for jobseekers, including graduates and working youths, under the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: MCCY and NYC will also set up a "YouthTech" programme to equip 1,000 youths, in the first instance, with digital skills and training, and then deploy them into the community and social service sector to help this sector to upskill and to digitalise.

sections.label: Youth partnerships on issues
sections.summary: Partnerships with youths will be expanded through projects such as the Youth Mental Well-being Network and a Youth Circle with MSE.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We will expand our partnerships with youths on these and other issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We have been working with youths through projects such as the Youth Mental Well-being Network, which was launched earlier this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We have started a Youth Circle with MSE to partner youths to create proposals and workable solutions that can improve our environment and enhance sustainability for the long term.

sections.label: Founders' Memorial and Citizenship Journey
sections.summary: Over 80,000 people contributed ideas to the Founders' Memorial, and 74 Singaporeans worked on the Singapore Citizenship Journey.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: More than 80,000 people of all ages have contributed their ideas and views to the Founders' Memorial to date, on how best to honour our past and create a beacon of inspiration, for our future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This year, 74 Singaporeans aged between 17 and 73 – a fairly broad spectrum of almost six decades – have come together to discuss and put together what they think every Singaporean ought to know, and create content to update the Singapore Citizenship Journey for new citizens.

sections.label: Meritocracy and structural inequality
sections.summary: Forces that enabled Boomers and Gen X to progress should not stratify society, so meritocracy must not become structural inequality.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The forces that enabled the Boomers and Gen X to progress ought not be allowed to stratify society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We must therefore work hard to ensure that meritocracy does not develop into structural inequality.

sections.label: Race-blind society aspiration
sections.summary: Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about becoming a race-blind society, an aspiration shared while recognising each race's individuality and diversity behind a common Singapore identity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Ms Sylvia Lim, on Tuesday, spoke about becoming a race-blind society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We share the same aspiration, recognising the individuality of each of our races, but at the same time, reaping the strength in that diversity behind the common Singapore identity.

sections.label: Intrusive policies and EIP
sections.summary: Senior Minister Tharman described the gamut of policies and programmes as the most intrusive, and the EIP as the most important social policy and greatest strength.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The whole gamut of policies and programmes that Senior Minister Tharman once famously described as the "most intrusive".

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And amongst them, the EIP, which Senior Minister Tharman described as our "most important" social policy, and our "greatest strength".

sections.label: Discrimination a lived reality
sections.summary: Discrimination remains a viscerally lived reality for some, as Faisal Manap and Carrie Tan pointed out, and ways to do better must continue to be found.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Yes, we are by no means perfect and discrimination remains a viscerally `rt lived reality for some, as hon Members Faisal Manap and Carrie Tan have pointed out earlier, and we must always continue to find ways to do better.

sections.label: Ethnic self-help groups serve vulnerable
sections.summary: The ethnic self-help groups rallied their respective communities to serve the more vulnerable across the spectrum of race and ethnicity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The ethnic self-help groups or SHGs have rallied their respective communities to serve the more vulnerable across the spectrum of race and ethnicity.

sections.label: MENDAKI non-Malay volunteers
sections.summary: Almost a quarter of the volunteers at MENDAKI today are not from the Malay race.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Almost a quarter of the volunteers at MENDAKI today are not from the Malay race.

sections.label: MCCY master plans and shared beliefs
sections.summary: The SG Arts Plan, SG Heritage Plan and Sports Vision 2030 are master plans MCCY will work on with Singaporeans, forged from shared beliefs including multiracialism and meritocracy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Our SG Arts Plan, SG Heritage Plan and Sports Vision 2030 are just some of the master plans that MCCY will be working on with Singaporeans from all walks of life to build a better home together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Our country has been forged from our shared belief in the tenets of democracy, multi-culturalism, multiracialism, religious harmony, rule of law and meritocracy.

sections.label: Singapore Tapestry and Youth Optimism
sections.summary: The passage describes the Singapore Tapestry as embodying Singapore's heart and spirit, and encourages youth to stay committed to their goals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In our case, I think it is the heart and spirit of Singapore which is embodied by the Singapore Tapestry – a tapestry that is woven out of diversity and adversity, its colours brightened by the idealism and energy of our youth, its threads tightly bound by a shared sense of community, culture and, ultimately, destiny.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Do not stop dreaming and never lose that youthful sense of optimism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This is not a lost generation despite what some have said.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: This, in fact, is a generation of opportunity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Whether you want to be an engineer or a dancer, a sports man or woman, a doctor or a content creator, stay true and committed to your goals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We will work with you to realise your dreams.

sections.label: Ethnic Integration Policy Economic Hardship
sections.summary: The passage raises concern that economic hardship for minority families under the Ethnic Integration Policy could cause festering resentment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: About the Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP), we all know the avowed purposes of it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But I think he will also agree and probably has come across cases where there is economic hardship caused to minority families due to the nature of the limitations placed on them when they try to sell their flats.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My concern is that if the unfairness is not addressed, the resentment might fester and in fact it might become quite a dangerous problem.

sections.label: Call to Adjust Ethnic Integration Policy
sections.summary: The passage asks the Government to review the Ethnic Integration Policy, citing families losing out economically when quotas are reached.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I think if there were to be different competing priorities, may I ask that the Government look at the EIP as it is implemented now.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I think there are many cases where families have lost out economically significantly, due to the quotas being reached.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: As I said, I believe that this policy needs to be adjusted if it is not abolished.

sections.label: Income and Education Progress
sections.summary: The passage states median income rose 32% in real terms over the last decade and post-secondary education rose from 22% to 79%.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Over the last decade, median income has increased by 32% in real terms – a substantial increase.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: While only 22% of those born in the 1940s progressed to post-Secondary education, 79% of those born in the 1970s did so.

sections.label: MOF Study on Income Mobility
sections.summary: The passage cites an MOF study showing about 14% of those with parents in the last income quintile reach the top quintile.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: A study by MOF has shown that in Singapore, about 14% of those with parents who were in the last income quintile when they were growing up, end up in the top quintile of income earners as adults.

sections.label: Gini Coefficient and Social Mobility
sections.summary: The passage states last year's Gini coefficient of 0.398 after taxes and transfers was the lowest in almost two decades.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Last year, our Gini coefficient of 0.398, after taxes and transfers, was at its lowest in almost two decades.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: But reducing inequality and sustaining social mobility will get more difficult with time.

sections.label: Low-income family education costs
sections.summary: Low-income families pay as low as $3 monthly for childcare and zero school fees, with reduced polytechnic and university fees.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Low-income families, including those living in HDB rental flats or receiving ComCare assistance, pay as low as $3 per month for full-day childcare at Anchor Operator pre-schools.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: They also pay zero school fees for Primary, Secondary, Pre-University, and ITE education, and receive additional support for other school expenses.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: The cash outlay for fees for low-income students has been brought down to $150 a year for Polytechnics, and $2,000 a year for most undergraduate courses.

sections.label: Healthcare and housing subsidies
sections.summary: Public healthcare is subsidised up to 80% with MediFund help, and housing subsidies let most first-timer families pay mortgages via CPF.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Public healthcare today is heavily subsidised – up to 80% – and those who are still unable to afford their bills can apply for MediFund assistance.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: We have one of the highest rates of home ownership around the world and provide significant housing subsidies – such that the majority of first-timer families can pay their mortgage instalments using CPF, with little or no cash outlay.

sections.label: University cohort participation rate
sections.summary: Autonomous University CPR was 27% in 2012 and is expected to exceed 40% this year, with another 10% for working adults.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Our Autonomous University Cohort Participation Rate, or CPR, was 27% in 2012.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: This year, we expect it to increase beyond the originally planned 40%, by up to two percentage points.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Around one in three students admitted to our Autonomous Universities today are Polytechnic graduates, up from one in four in 2012.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: On top of this 40% CPR, we also cater another 10% for working adults to upgrade to a university degree.

sections.label: Government-supported pre-school places
sections.summary: By 2025, 80% of pre-schoolers will have a place in a Government-supported pre-school, up from just over 50% today.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: By 2025, 80% of pre-schoolers will have a place in a Government-supported pre-school, up from just over 50% today.

sections.label: Values of a society of opportunity
sections.summary: A society of opportunity must be undergirded by egalitarianism, humility, and responsibility.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: A society of opportunity must be undergirded by: first, egalitarianism – where we treat everyone as equals regardless of their background, with respect and dignity; second, humility – where we recognise that our achievements in life are not just our own, but those of our families and the communities that have supported us; third, responsibility – where we care for not just ourselves, but for our fellow man and our environment.

sections.label: Racial and religious harmony
sections.summary: Building a fair and equitable society requires strengthening racial and religious harmony and a multicultural ethos, including race-blind ideals.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: What is core to building a fair and equitable society is to strengthen our racial and religious harmony, and our multicultural ethos.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: We all want the ideals of a "race-blind" society, one where there is no racial prejudice and discrimination in our attitudes and practices, including in the way we treat one another, and select people for jobs.

sections.label: Racial and Singaporean identity
sections.summary: Having a strong racial identity and a strong Singaporean identity are not contradictory, and the CMIO framework does not affect how Singaporean one is.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Second, from our own individual experiences, as well as psychological research, we know that there is in fact no inherent contradiction for an individual to have both a strong racial identity and a strong Singaporean identity.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: On the contrary, to be truly Singaporean is to understand and respect these race differences.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: So, having the CMIO framework does not make us less Singaporean and doing away with it does not mean we will become more Singaporean either.

sections.label: Egypt leaders praise Malay/Muslim community
sections.summary: During Minister Masagos' visit to Egypt, the Grand Imam of Al Azhar and the Grand Mufti described Singapore's Malay/Muslim community as a model minority.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Last year during Minister Masagos’ official visit to Egypt, the Grand Imam of Al Azhar and the Grand Mufti of Egypt shared their views that our Malay/Muslim community is the model of a successful minority Muslim community living and functioning in a plural society.

sections.label: Committee on Future Asatizah
sections.summary: The speaker chaired COFA last year to transform the religious sector so religious teachers keep pace with developments in science, demographics and socio-economic issues.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Mr Fahmi Aliman asked about the importance of equipping our future religious leaders with the right skills, so that they can provide strong guidance to the community within our country's unique context.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: That is why I chaired the Committee on Future Asatizah, or COFA, last year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: COFA looks into transforming the religious sector, to ensure that our religious teachers keep pace with the latest developments in science, in our demographics and socio-economic issues, and its effect on the community.

sections.label: Asatizah guidance on COVID-19
sections.summary: The Office of the Mufti and senior asatizah worked with medical professionals to issue religious guidance on suspending Friday prayers and deferring the Haj pilgrimage.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: The Office of the Mufti and our senior asatizah worked with medical professionals, demonstrating their confidence and leadership in issuing religious guidance on issues such as the suspension of Friday prayers in the mosques and deferring this year's Haj pilgrimage.

sections.label: Malay educational and job progress
sections.summary: Over 90% of Malay students attained post-secondary education, first class honours multiplied ten times in seven years, and one in three workers are in PMET jobs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: For instance, now more than 90% of Malay students in each cohort attained post-secondary education; the number of those who attained first class honours multiplied 10 times in 7 years; one in three of our workers are in PMET jobs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: For children of these families, we will strengthen our support through UPLIFT, managed by the Ministry of Education, in collaboration with the Ministry of Social and Family Development.

sections.label: Mendaki SENSE JUMP career fair
sections.summary: Mendaki SENSE's JUMP virtual career fair offered over 3,000 vacancies, received more than 10,000 applications and placed 600 job seekers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: For example, Mendaki SENSE organised the JUMP virtual career fair which offered more than 3,000 job vacancies across various sectors.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: More than 10,000 job applications have been received and 600 job seekers have been successfully placed into jobs so far.

sections.label: COVID-19 community support funds
sections.summary: Muis administered a COVID-19 support fund and MENDAKI allocated $1.9 million for students' learning and ITE allowances.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: For instance, with the support of community contributions, Muis administered the COVID-19 Muis Support Fund to support those within the community who face severe financial hardships due to the pandemic.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: MENDAKI has allocated $1.9 million to support, among other things, students' Home-Based Learning by leasing laptops, and providing interim allowance to ITE students who have lost their part-time jobs or if their families had income loss amid the pandemic.

sections.label: Defining basic commitment and trade-offs
sections.summary: Singapore must define its basic commitment to citizens, make trade-offs, and build psychological capital to emerge stronger.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: We will need to decide how to define the basic commitment that we will provide all citizens what our aspirations are for ourselves and for our society, and how best to get there.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: We will have to make difficult trade-offs, in how we allocate limited resources among competing needs, and balance across conflicting objectives.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: We will need courage to make tough decisions, boldness to change the status quo, and humility to listen to feedback and suggestions to improve.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Above all, we must continue to put the interests of Singapore and the well-being of Singaporeans first.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: We will need to build an environment that not only supports us to seize opportunities, but also equips us with what behavioural science calls “psychological capital” – the self-efficacy, optimism, hope and resilience – that we need, to adapt and emerge stronger and better.

sections.label: Harmonious society in education and workplace
sections.summary: Success in harmonious living must be translated into education, workplace and society, where differences strengthen the nation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Education and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
sentences.text: Our success in creating a society where people of different backgrounds live harmoniously must be translated into our education system, our workplace, and indeed, our society, where what makes us different individually, makes us stronger as a nation.

sections.label: One national umbrella for self-help
sections.summary: A speaker asks whether community expertise in self-help groups could be brought under one national umbrella.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I do not think any of us is pretending that we are ethnically uniform or that there are no racial differences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: But I wanted to ask him whether, for the community expertise that he mentioned that is in the self-help groups, is it not possible to bring everybody under one national umbrella so that we do not lose that expertise in that sense?

sections.label: Self-help group concept longevity
sections.summary: The self-help group concept has worked for almost 40 years.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: The self-help group concept has worked for over almost 40 years now.

sections.label: Space for each community's issues
sections.summary: Each community should have space to understand its own issues and challenges rather than one race-blind fund.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: Because we do understand our cultural nuances, we do understand our cultural history, we do understand what we stand for as individual communities.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: So, I think it is not about whether we want to pull everybody together and just have one race-blind fund, but it is also to be able to give each community the space to understand their respective issues, their respective challenges, work in their own pace and find their own strengths.

sections.label: Tuition programme coordination
sections.summary: Children can join tuition classes run by CDAC, SINDA or MENDAKI based on where they live.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: Today, the tuition programme, for example, we have seen great coordination – any child who would like to participate in any of the tuition classes can participate in a tuition class organised by CDAC, SINDA or MENDAKI based on the proximity of where he or she lives.

sections.label: Children of mixed marriages
sections.summary: Parents and children decide their own classification under the double-barrelled classification policy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: My question is: how will the Government adapt to these changing realities?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Would children who are offsprings of such marriages be asked to classify themselves as "Others", or how would that be approached?

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: I think as the Member has rightly put it already, they are allowed to decide for themselves.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: The parents are allowed to decide for themselves because of the double-barrelled classification policy that we have put in place.

sections.label: Children choosing identity
sections.summary: The double-barrelled policy lets children decide which identity they want to take up.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: I think that provides diversity for the child growing up in such a family.

sentences.speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
sentences.text: So, I will leave it to the children and the double-barrelled policy allow them to make the decision on which identity they want to take up.

sections.label: Self-help groups and amalgamation
sections.summary: The speaker acknowledged self-help groups' work and asked whether amalgamation could achieve similar or better outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: First of all, in my speech, I had acknowledged the good work done by the self-help groups, especially for the under-privileged and children in particular.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: But the question, of course, is whether similar outcomes or even better outcomes can be achieved with an amalgamation.

sections.label: Existing non ethnic-based bodies
sections.summary: Several non ethnic-based bodies exist, including OnePeople.sg, and the speaker suggests working with existing bodies.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: In fact, we have several such bodies that exist that engage in non ethnic-based help, across a number of communities, across a number of causes, across a number of ages.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: This includes the People's Association (PA) – and I know Ms Sylvia Lim and her colleagues have particular views of the PA but it is not limited to the PA.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: But one of those bodies was actually founded by the self-help groups coming together several years ago and we celebrated our 10th anniversary a few years ago; I happen to be the Chairman of OnePeople.sg.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Rather than talking about getting rid of existing bodies or creating new bodies, perhaps, we should work with the bodies that already exist.

sections.label: Self-help group deductions
sections.summary: Self-help groups are a Government-sanctioned network making monthly race-based deductions, which the speaker says deserves a second look.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I would be happy to make this the last point.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: But of course, one of the questions which I have and is part of my suggestion, is that currently, the self-help groups are a Government-sanctioned network that makes monthly deductions from Singaporeans on a race basis.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
